Levers:
A lever is a stiff bar that turns around a fixed point called the fulcrum. The effort is the force you apply, and the load is the force you overcome. The law of the lever: effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so F1 × d1 = F2 × d2.

There are three classes. In a first class lever the fulcrum is in the middle (seesaw). In a second class lever the load is in the middle (wheelbarrow). In a third class lever the effort is in the middle (tweezers). A long effort arm gives a small effort but a longer movement.
Pulleys and inclined planes:
A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the force, so its mechanical advantage is 1. A movable pulley is held by two rope segments, so the effort is half of the load. In a pulley system with n supporting segments, the ideal effort is load / n, but the rope is pulled n times farther.

An inclined plane is a ramp. Without friction, effort = load × height / length, and the mechanical advantage is length / height. A longer ramp needs less force but more distance. The work stays the same.
Gears and wheel and axle:
A wheel and axle has a large wheel and a small axle that turn together. Its mechanical advantage is wheel radius / axle radius when the effort acts on the wheel.

Gears are wheels with teeth. The driver gear turns the driven gear, and meshing gears turn in opposite directions. Gear ratio = driven teeth / driver teeth. Speed of driven gear = driver speed × driver teeth / driven teeth. A larger driven gear turns slower but gives more torque.
Work and torque:
Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force: W = F × d. The unit is the joule (J), and 1 J = 1 N·m. If the object does not move, the work is zero. Power is the rate of work: P = W / t, measured in watts (W).

Torque is the turning effect of a force: torque = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the turning point. Its unit is the newton meter (N·m). A longer wrench gives a larger torque for the same force.
Mechanical advantage and efficiency:
Mechanical advantage (MA) = load / effort. It is a ratio with no unit. The ideal MA comes from the machine's shape and ignores friction. The actual MA is smaller because of friction.

Work input = effort × effort distance. Work output = load × load distance. Efficiency = useful work output / work input × 100%. A real machine always has an efficiency below 100%, because some energy becomes heat. A machine cannot create energy.
